items.name: Vocal thinking in instrumental writing
items.description: Every melody could be sung. The line breathes naturally, has an identifiable phrase shape (rise → peak → cadential fall), and never asks the instrument to do something a good singer couldn't do. The p

items.name: Chromatic inflection for emotional nuance
items.description: A single chromatic note (lowered 6th, raised 4th, Neapolitan chord) colors the emotional temperature of the phrase. Not a modulation — one note reveals everything.

items.name: Transparent, chamber-like texture
items.description: Each instrument's role is distinct. Mozart thins deliberately, letting single instruments emerge.

items.name: Symmetrical phrase structure subverted at one moment
items.description: 4-bar phrases balance each other, but once per section a phrase extends (4+4 becomes 4+5) or elides. This surprise makes the symmetry around it more satisfying.

items.name: Minor-mode shadow in major contexts
items.description: A sudden shift to parallel minor that passes like a cloud. The return to major feels like relief.

items.name: Monothematic sonata form
items.description: In many Haydn movements, the "second theme" is actually a transformation of the first theme — not a contrasting melody but the same melody in a new harmonic context. The listener expects contrast; Hay

items.name: Motivic cell driving everything

items.period: Middle Period (the most requested — Op.59, Symphony 5, Waldstein, Appassionata)

items.name: Sudden dynamic contrasts
items.description: Subito piano after forte, or sforzando on unexpected beats. Not gradual crescendos — shocking contrasts. The sfz is placed off the downbeat to destabilize the meter.
items.period: Middle Period (the most requested — Op.59, Symphony 5, Waldstein, Appassionata)

items.name: Modal mixture as drama
items.description: bVI, bVII, iv in major contexts. The shift to the parallel minor is a dramatic event. The return to major after minor feels like genuine triumph, not just harmonic convenience.
items.period: Middle Period (the most requested — Op.59, Symphony 5, Waldstein, Appassionata)

items.name: Sustained development that escalates
items.description: Development sections don't wander; they build. Each sequence iteration is louder, higher, more harmonically intense. A 64-bar development should feel like it's physically arriving somewhere.
items.period: Middle Period (the most requested — Op.59, Symphony 5, Waldstein, Appassionata)

items.name: False recapitulation / structural deception

items.period: Middle Period (the most requested — Op.59, Symphony 5, Waldstein, Appassionata)

items.name: Fugue as struggle
items.description: Fugue appears not as Baroque exercise but as expression of psychological conflict. The counterpoint is tight, the entries overlapping, the texture dense. It *strains*.

items.name: Variation as transcendence
items.description: A simple theme is varied into something barely recognizable — ornamented to pure filigree, stripped to skeleton, inverted, fugued, absorbed into a new world. Each variation moves further from the them

items.name: Radical harmonic relationship
items.description: Key changes that skip traditional pivot chords: C major to Db major (a semitone), or C major to A major (a third) directly. These arrive without preparation.

items.name: Extreme register contrasts
items.description: Very high + very low simultaneously with a gap between them. Or a melody that descends into the bass register unexpectedly. Or a single high note held against a dense low cluster.

items.name: Rests as structural events
items.description: Silences that last more than a bar, placed at dramatic peaks. The silence IS the climax, not the note before or after it.
